projects.title: Le Grand Ciné
projects.outcome: An identity that holds a poster without overwhelming the hotel it sits inside.
projects.summary: A cinema inside a luxury hotel, so the identity had to carry the emotional pull of film and the restraint of hospitality at once.
projects.body:
## The problem

Le Grand Cinéma sits inside a hotel, which pulls the identity two ways. Cinema branding wants drama. Hospitality branding wants restraint. Too far either way and it either cheapens the hotel or disappears inside it.

## What I did

The brief was a bold, cinematic identity that captured both the luxury of the hotel experience and the emotional impact of film, while staying sleek, modern and usable across mediums.

The mark is built on a lion, cinema's oldest visual shorthand, paired with film strip geometry, in deep red and black so it reads premium rather than loud.

The test throughout was scale. A cinema identity lives on a ticket stub, a poster, an illuminated sign and a screen. Anything that only worked large got cut.

## The result

An identity that holds its own on a poster without competing with the hotel around it.

projects.title: True North
projects.outcome: 210+ survey responses turned into a full accessible booking app, researched and designed solo in two months.
projects.summary: Travel booking is scattered across a dozen tabs and the fees only appear at the end. I set out to find whether that frustration was mine alone, then designed the alternative.
projects.services: All in one travel app covering flights, hotels, trains and rentals. UX centric reservation platform.
projects.body:
## The problem

Booking a trip means holding a dozen tabs open and still not trusting the total. The brief I set myself was to solve the biggest pain points people hit when booking online, on platforms like Booking and Airbnb. But suspicion is not research.

## Finding out

A bilingual survey returned **210+ responses** from travellers in Algeria and abroad, across a wide spread of ages and backgrounds. Three frustrations came back repeatedly:

- **Hidden fees** that only surface at the final step
- **Search filtering** too coarse to narrow anything down
- **Availability** that contradicts itself between screens

I then worked through **10+ platforms**, using them directly and reading their App Store reviews, which is where people say what they actually think. That became three personas with empathy maps, and functional and visual requirements written before anything was drawn.

## Designing it

| Decision | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Lexend for all text | Built for reading ease, dyslexia friendly |
| Blues with one warm accent | Travel familiar, one colour reserved for action |
| 48px touch targets | Comfortable on a phone, meets WCAG guidance |
| Dark mode from the start | Retrofitting contrast never goes well |
| English and French | The audience was bilingual |

Accessibility drove the visual decisions rather than being audited at the end: **WCAG AA and AAA contrast**, matching type sizing, and layouts that survive being scaled up.

## What it produced

A complete high fidelity app covering flights, hotels, trains and rentals, a full Figma UI kit and prototype documented for hand-off, bilingual and accessible with dark mode.

## What I took from it

Research surfaces frustrations you would never guess at from a desk. Accessibility is not a constraint on good design, it _is_ the design.

Built alone, in two months, alongside a full time job.

projects.body:
## The problem

Researchers have to trust DiData before they put anything sensitive into it, and the identity did not carry that weight. Colour and structure drifted between product, decks and marketing, so every touchpoint looked like a different company.

## The constraint

Existing clients already recognised the logo. Starting over would have cost that recognition, so the brief was refinement rather than replacement: adjust colour and structure for better clarity, contrast and consistency while keeping the original mark recognisable.

A tighter brief, and a more interesting one.

## What I did

I kept the mark and rebuilt around it, then wrote a full graphic charter so the rules existed outside my head and the team could apply them without me.

## The result

One visual language across every touchpoint, and a charter that outlasted my involvement.

projects.title: Wassal / TourniPOS, Rebranding
projects.outcome: An identity legible at 48 pixels and AAA rated for contrast, plus a lesson in defending design decisions.
projects.summary: A point of sale app for mobile vendors, who hand it their day's takings before they trust it.
projects.body:
## The problem

TourniPOS is a POS app built for direct sales and mobile vendors: small business owners in food, cosmetics and cleaning products, most working mobile or semi mobile. The brief was a modern, trustworthy identity that reflected the app's flexibility, clarity and productivity, while appealing to a wide range of owners who are not technical.

They are handing the app their sales and stock. It has to look dependable without looking corporate.

## What I did

**The mark** is a simplified 3D truck whose back is shaped like a paper receipt, logistics and record keeping in one form. It says what the app does before a word is read, and holds at app icon size.

**Colour** runs on deep navy for trust, with lighter blues for clarity. Contrast is **AAA rated**, so it is accessible as well as screen ready.

**Type** pairs Reddit Sans for Latin with Tajawal for Arabic, both modern and highly legible, keeping tone consistent across two scripts.

**The system** covers brand safe spacing, minimum sizing rules and mockups for every use case.

## What actually happened

The final direction was never implemented.

The difficulty was not technical. It was sustained misalignment with stakeholders about what the brand needed to do. Holding the identity together across shifting expectations took constant iteration and a lot of restraint.

I include it because the work is good and the lesson was worth more than a smooth project would have been: communicate the reasoning early, structure decisions so they can be revisited without starting over, and be able to defend a choice on grounds other than taste.

projects.body:
## The problem

Language brands fall into one of two traps: playful to the point of looking like a children's app, or so formal they feel like homework. Golexy's audience is adults choosing to learn, so they need encouragement, not either extreme.

## What I did

The brief was a unique and meaningful identity reflecting three values the platform runs on: creativity, trust and educational excellence.

projects.title: Confirmoo, UX Audit
projects.outcome: An audit across ten methods that became the brief for both redesigns that followed.
projects.summary: A capable product that users could not describe. Before redesigning anything, I needed to find exactly where it lost them.
projects.services: Navigation and IA, feature hierarchy, content clarity, accessibility, localisation
projects.body:
## The problem

Confirmoo's software did a lot, and merchants could not explain what it was. Visitors read the site and left without understanding the offer. The instinct was to redesign. Mine was to find out what was actually broken first.

The brief was to evaluate usability, clarity and overall experience across both the marketing site and the software, identify friction points, and define clear improvements to support a full redesign of both.

## How I audited it

Ten methods, chosen so the findings would hold up to challenge: heuristic evaluation against Nielsen's principles, information architecture review, navigation flow mapping, UX copy and content strategy, micro interaction and motion audit, performance as experience, WCAG accessibility checks, user journey analysis, and competitor benchmarking both local and international.

Inputs were the marketing site, the web app, stakeholder context, real merchant use cases, and content in **three languages**: English, French and Arabic.

## What I found

**Navigation was structurally broken.** Anchor links jumped to the wrong sections. About, Features and Pricing all returned to the hero. Nothing indicated where you were.

**The architecture worked against the user.** Duplicate footer links, pages existing as both sections and destinations, and an order following internal company logic rather than a visitor's.

**The messaging never said what the product was.** The hero did not explain it, About was dense, features were generic rather than merchant specific, and pricing gave no basis for judging value.

**Interaction and performance undercut the rest.** Scroll jitter, slow images, missing transitions, components differing between pages.

**Localisation was inconsistent**, and not adapted for Algerian merchants specifically.

## Why it mattered

The audit turned "it feels wrong" into a specific, ordered list, so both redesigns solved identified problems instead of guessing.
